video.title: Allah’s Mercy Is Greater Than All Your Sins
video.creator: FreeQuranEducation

summary.headline: All three claims trace to authentic Qur'anic and Hadith sources.
summary.note: This video relays three well-known Hadith Qudsi accurately. No weak or fabricated narrations were detected, and one claim is grounded directly in the Qur'an.

claims.originalQuote: Allah descends to the lowest heaven in the last third of the night and asks who is calling upon Him so He can answer.
claims.normalizedClaim: Allah descends to the lowest heaven during the last third of the night to answer the supplications of His servants.

sahih.excerpt: Our Lord, the Blessed, the Superior, comes every night down on the nearest Heaven to us when the last third of the night remains...
Allah descends every night to the lowest heaven when one-third of the first part of the night is over...
The Lord Almighty descends to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains...
Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, descends to the lowest heaven...

hasan.excerpt: Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven...
Allah descends to the lowest heaven...
hasan.gradingNote: Hasan. Lower entailment as it focuses purely on the descent rather than the call/response.

claims.originalQuote: Nothing can change your destiny or Qadar except your dua.
claims.normalizedClaim: Supplication (Dua) is the only thing that can alter the Divine Decree (Qadar).

hasan.excerpt: Nothing turns back the Decree except supplication, and nothing increases life span except righteousness.
Nothing repels the decree except supplication...
A man is deprived of provision because of a sin he commits. Nothing repels the decree except supplication...
Caution does not save from the decree, but supplication benefits against what has been decreed and what has not been decreed.
hasan.gradingNote: Graded Hasan by some scholars; corroborates the main claim indirectly.

hasan.excerpt: Supplication is beneficial regarding things that have already happened and things that have not yet happened.
hasan.gradingNote: Hasan; provides partial entailment (60%) to the overarching concept of Dua actively affecting decree without using the explicit 'nothing changes' language.

claims.originalQuote: Dua is the essence of worship.
claims.normalizedClaim: Supplication (Dua) is intrinsically linked to, or constitutes the core essence of, worship in Islam.

quran.excerpt: And your Lord says, 'Call upon Me; I will respond to you.' Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell [rendered] contemptible.
quran.gradingNote: Definitive (qaṭ'ī). Establishes Dua as practically synonymous with worship.

sahih.excerpt: The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: Supplication is worship.
Supplication is worship. Then he recited: 'And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will answer you.'
The Messenger of Allah said, 'Indeed, supplication is worship.'

hasan.excerpt: The Messenger of Allah said: 'There is nothing more honorable to Allah than supplication.'
hasan.gradingNote: Hasan (Darussalam). Provides partial entailment (65%) indicating the high overarching status of Dua in worship.

hasan.excerpt: Supplication is the essence of worship.
hasan.gradingNote: Often cited as the exact quote, though its specific chain is considered Da'if (weak) by some, it heavily entails the original quote contextually.

video.title: We've all done this — a friend stops a gossip session before it starts
video.creator: Browniesaadi

summary.headline: All two claims align with established Qur'anic verses and authenticated Hadith on backbiting, talebearing, and the discord they cause.
summary.note: This skit accurately reflects mainstream Islamic teaching: gheebah (backbiting) and namimah (talebearing) are both classified as major sins, and namimah is repeatedly singled out — including in a hadith about punishment in the grave — as a cause of broken relationships and fitna. One nuance worth flagging: scholars recognize six narrow, necessity-based exceptions to the backbiting prohibition (e.g. reporting oppression to someone who can fix it, seeking a religious ruling). The video states the rule as an absolute, which is the common simplified framing but not the complete fiqh picture.

claims.originalQuote: You're about to commit a major sin in Islam. Gossiping... is actually a major sin.
claims.normalizedClaim: Speaking about someone behind their back in a way they would dislike (gheebah/backbiting) is treated as a major sin in Islam, even when the statement is factually true.

quran.excerpt: And do not backbite one another. Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would detest it.
quran.gradingNote: Definitive (qaṭ'ī) — established Qur'anic text; the primary proof-text scholars cite when discussing gheebah.

quran.excerpt: Woe to every scorner and slanderer.
quran.gradingNote: Definitive Qur'anic text, though 'humazah/lumazah' is a broader term for defamation by word and gesture, not gheebah specifically — Ibn Kathir links it to the same family of sins.

sahih.excerpt: Do you know what backbiting is? ... It is to mention your brother in a way he dislikes. ... If what you say about him is true, you have backbitten him; if it is not true, you have slandered him.
sahih.gradingNote: Sahih, recorded by Muslim — the foundational hadith that defines gheebah.

sahih.excerpt: The real bankrupt of my Ummah is the one who comes on the Day of Resurrection with prayer, fasting, and charity, but comes having abused this one, slandered that one... so his good deeds are given away, and if they run out, the sins of those he wronged are loaded onto him.
sahih.gradingNote: Sahih; establishes the severity of backbiting via its cost on Judgment Day, supporting the 'major sin' classification rather than defining the act itself.

sahih.excerpt: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say good or remain silent.
sahih.gradingNote: Muttafaq 'Alayh; a general principle about guarding speech rather than a direct ruling on gheebah — supports but doesn't independently establish the claim.

hasan.reference: Riyad al-Salihin, Ch. 256 (Imam Nawawi, summarizing scholarly ijma')
hasan.narrator: Scholarly consensus, not a hadith narration
hasan.excerpt: Backbiting is permissible only for a legitimate Shari'ah purpose unattainable without it — six such purposes: reporting an injustice, seeking help to correct a wrong, requesting a religious ruling, warning Muslims of harm, naming an open sinner, and identification by a known trait.
hasan.gradingNote: Not a hadith itself but a near-unanimous fiqh ruling. It doesn't contradict the prohibition — it qualifies it. Included because the video states the rule as an unqualified blanket prohibition, which omits these recognized exceptions.

claims.originalQuote: Telling people what others said about them to cause fitna is actually a major sin.
claims.normalizedClaim: Carrying tales between people, specifically repeating what one person said about another with the effect or intent of stirring conflict (namimah) major sin in Islam.

quran.excerpt: A habitual faultfinder, going about with malicious gossip (namīm).
quran.gradingNote: Definitive Qur'anic text naming namimah explicitly as a trait of a corrupt character.

sahih.excerpt: The qattat (talebearer) will not enter Paradise.
sahih.gradingNote: Muttafaq 'Alayh — agreed upon by Bukhari and Muslim, the highest tier of authenticity. 'Qattat' is the classical term for someone who relays what was said in order to cause harm.

sahih.excerpt: These two are being punished, but not for anything difficult to avoid. One of them did not guard himself from his urine; the other used to go about with namimah, to cause enmity between people.
sahih.gradingNote: Muttafaq 'Alayh; one of the two men punished in his grave is explicitly described as a talebearer who stirred enmity between friends — directly matches the video's description.

sahih.excerpt: ...going about between people, spreading words to corrupt their relationships.
sahih.gradingNote: Graded Sahih by Al-Albani; from Bukhari's separate compilation on manners, slightly outside the two Sahihayn but still authenticated.

hasan.reference: Sahih al-Targhib wa't-Tarhib 2824 (compiled & graded by Al-Albani)
hasan.excerpt: The worst of Allah's slaves are the talebearers, who cause separation between those who love each other and seek out faults for the blameless.
hasan.gradingNote: Hasan; graded by Al-Albani from multiple supporting chains. Closely matches the video's description of namimah as deliberately stirring conflict.

video.title: SEEK knowledge even in China
video.creator: Unverified — channel tags include #abaalsadiq, #imammahdi (could not independently confirm channel identity)

summary.headline: The central prophetic attribution is built on a hadith that mainstream hadith critics classify as fabricated or extremely weak; the speaker's extension of it to mean 'seek knowledge from non-Muslims' goes further than even the disputed source text itself was ever understood to mean.
summary.note: The phrase 'seek knowledge even if it were in China' is one of the most famous examples of a popularly-quoted hadith with a poor isnad (chain of transmission). It traces back almost entirely through a single defective route — al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyyah, from Abu 'Atikah Tarif ibn Salman, from Anas ibn Malik — and Abu 'Atikah is independently graded matruk ('abandoned') by hadith critics. Ibn Hibban (d. 354H) ruled it has no basis (la asl) and is batil (false/baseless); Ibn al-Jawzi placed it in his Kitab al-Mawdu'at (Book of Fabricated Hadith); and the modern critic Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani independently graded it mawdu' (fabricated) in Da'if al-Jami' al-Saghir, no. 906. A minority view (al-Mizzi, followed by al-Suyuti) argued that because the saying exists in roughly 50 independent weak chains, the cumulative weight raises it to hasan li-ghayrihi — but specialists who traced those chains note this corroboration argument applies to the shorter wording 'seeking knowledge is obligatory upon every Muslim' (which IS authentically and separately established, e.g. Sunan Ibn Majah 224, graded Sahih by al-Albani), not to the distinctive 'even in China' clause, whose supporting chains are independently riddled with narrators accused of lying or fabrication. Separately, even scholars who treated the saying as usable (e.g. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, al-Munawi) historically read 'China' as rhetorical hyperbole for the lengths a hadith-collector should go to verify a chain of transmission within the Muslim scholarly tradition — not as license to source religious knowledge from non-Muslims, which is the speaker's own added extension in the second half of the video.

stats.firstSeen: Not tracked — illustrative fields only; no real usage telemetry exists for this entry

claims.originalQuote: they ... want to follow the words of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ when he said seek knowledge even if it were in China
claims.normalizedClaim: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ authentically said, 'Seek knowledge even if it were in China,' making this a genuine prophetic command (hadith).

quran.excerpt: Say, 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge.'
quran.gradingNote: Definitive Qur'anic text establishing the general virtue of seeking knowledge. Provides background support for the spirit of the video but says nothing about China, distance, or non-Muslim sources, so it cannot independently support the specific prophetic attribution being made.

sahih.excerpt: Seeking knowledge is obligatory upon every Muslim.
sahih.gradingNote: Graded Sahih by al-Albani (Sahih Sunan Ibn Majah; also Sahih al-Jami' al-Saghir 3913-4) based on the cumulative weight of dozens of weak corroborating chains noted by al-Mizzi. Critically, this sahih grading covers ONLY this shorter wording — it does not extend to the separate, far weaker 'even if it were in China' clause that the video actually quotes.

sahih.excerpt: Whoever treads a path in search of knowledge, Allah would make that path easy, leading him to Paradise.
sahih.gradingNote: Sahih (Muslim). Establishes the general religious virtue of seeking knowledge but contains no geographic specification and is a textually distinct hadith from the China narration.

sahih.excerpt: Whomever Allah wants good for, He grants him understanding of the religion.
sahih.gradingNote: Muttafaq 'Alayh. Frames the praised 'knowledge' specifically as religious understanding (fiqh fi'l-din) — narrower and contextually different from the China hadith's open-ended phrasing. Offers indirect background only.

hasan.excerpt: Whoever takes a path upon which to obtain knowledge, Allah makes the path to Paradise easy for him.
hasan.gradingNote: Graded Hasan by al-Tirmidhi himself. Parallel wording to Sahih Muslim 2699a; again, no China or distance reference.

hasan.reference: Al-Mizzi (cited in al-Sakhawi, al-Maqasid al-Hasana) / al-Suyuti, al-La'ali al-Masnu'ah 1:193
hasan.narrator: Composite — corroborated across roughly 50 independently weak chains per al-Mizzi's count, via Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri
hasan.excerpt: Al-Mizzi and al-Suyuti argued that, taken collectively, the sheer number of independent weak chains raises the narration to hasan li-ghayrihi, rejecting Ibn al-Jawzi's fabrication ruling.
hasan.gradingNote: This is the strongest minority case for treating the saying as usable, and it meets only a borderline 60% entailment threshold. Even sympathetic reviewers (e.g. the chain study summarized on livingislam.org/Shaykh G.F. Haddad) note nearly all of the supporting chains for the 'China' clause specifically pass through narrators independently flagged as liars or hadith-fabricators — so quantity does not offset quality for this particular wording, even though it does for the shorter 'obligatory upon every Muslim' phrase.

maudu.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (chain: al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyyah ← Abu 'Atikah Tarif ibn Salman ← Anas)
maudu.excerpt: Seek knowledge even if it were in China, for seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
maudu.gradingNote: This is the primary chain underlying the 'China' wording, and al-Bayhaqi himself flags it as weak. Abu 'Atikah Tarif ibn Salman, the key narrator, is graded matruk ('abandoned' — his hadith are discarded), and Ibn 'Adi separately called this chain munkar al-hadith.

maudu.reference: Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, al-Rihlah fi Talab al-Hadith (opening chains, #1-3); Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, Jami' Bayan al-'Ilm wa Fadlih
maudu.excerpt: Seek knowledge even if it were in China, for seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
maudu.gradingNote: Graded da'if (weak) by Dr. Nur al-Din 'Itr in his critical study of al-Khatib's Rihlah. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr transmits the wording without vouching for its chain.

maudu.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (chain formally examined and rejected)
maudu.excerpt: Seek knowledge even if it were in China.
maudu.gradingNote: Ibn al-Jawzi formally classifies the 'China' narration as mawdu' (fabricated), following Ibn al-Qaysarani (d. 507H) — the first hadith critic on record to declare this specific wording forged, in his Ma'rifat al-Tadhkira, entry #118.

maudu.reference: Ibn Hibban, al-Majruhin (verdict preserved and discussed in later commentary literature, e.g. al-'Ajluni's Kashf al-Khafa)
maudu.narrator: Critical assessment of the Anas ibn Malik chain
maudu.excerpt: Ibn Hibban's ruling, in his own words as transmitted: there is no basis (la asl) for this wording through Ibn 'Umar, through Nafi', or through Malik ibn Anas — it is reported only via a single defective route through Anas, and it is batil.
maudu.gradingNote: Ibn Hibban (d. 354H), a foundational early critic of hadith narrators, gives one of the harshest verdicts available: baseless and false, not merely weak.

maudu.reference: Al-Albani, Da'if al-Jami' al-Saghir, no. 906; also discussed in Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Da'ifah
maudu.narrator: Verdict on the Anas ibn Malik narration
maudu.excerpt: Al-Albani's recorded verdict on this specific entry: mawdu' (fabricated).
maudu.gradingNote: The most widely-cited modern critical hadith scholar reaches the same fabrication conclusion as Ibn Hibban and Ibn al-Jawzi, while explicitly distinguishing the (fabricated) China clause from the (separately authentic) 'obligatory upon every Muslim' wording.

claims.originalQuote: that means like seek knowledge even outside of the Muslim sources outside of the Arab outside of the companions ... there's knowledge to be found in China ... and amongst the non-Arabs and perhaps even amongst the non-Muslims altogether
claims.normalizedClaim: The hadith 'seek knowledge even if it were in China' instructs Muslims to seek knowledge outside the Muslim and Arab tradition entirely, including from non-Muslim sources.

quran.excerpt: O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.
quran.gradingNote: Definitive Qur'anic text on human diversity and mutual acquaintance, sometimes invoked in support of cross-cultural exchange. Its primary subject is human kinship rather than a ruling on where religious or worldly knowledge should be sourced from, so it offers only loose, indirect support.

sahih.excerpt: Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say, 'We believe in Allah and whatever is revealed to us, and whatever is revealed to you.'
sahih.gradingNote: Sahih al-Bukhari (recorded in several chapters from the same narration). Establishes a deliberately cautious, neither-accept-nor-reject posture toward religious material coming from outside the Muslim community — in real tension with a reading of the video's claim that implies non-Muslim sources can simply be approached on the same footing as Islamic ones for religious knowledge.

hasan.excerpt: The word of wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he is most deserving of it.
hasan.gradingNote: Graded Hasan by al-Suyuti (al-Jami' al-Saghir), but assessed as da'if jiddan/munkar by Shaykh Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut, since the narrator Ibrahim ibn al-Fadl al-Makhzumi is graded matruk. Scholarly opinion is genuinely split between hasan (via corroborating routes) and very weak — this is the closest authentic-adjacent textual support for 'take wisdom from any source,' though it is itself a disputed narration, not a settled one.

hasan.reference: Nahj al-Balaghah, Saying 80 (attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib)
hasan.narrator: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (compiled without a formal isnad by al-Sharif al-Radi)
hasan.excerpt: Wisdom is the lost property of the believer, so take wisdom even from the people of hypocrisy.
hasan.gradingNote: Not a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ and not graded under the sahih/hasan/da'if isnad system the way Prophetic hadith are, since Nahj al-Balaghah sayings were compiled largely without chains. Included because it is the closest topical match to the video's specific claim — explicitly extending 'take wisdom' to outsiders — and is widely cited in Shi'a sources, which appears to match the apparent orientation of this channel.

maudu.narrator: Anas ibn Malik (chain via the matruk narrator Abu 'Atikah Tarif ibn Salman)
maudu.excerpt: Seek knowledge even if it were in China, for seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
maudu.gradingNote: Even taken at face value, the wording only commands seeking knowledge over distance — it says nothing explicit about non-Muslim sources, Arab vs. non-Arab origin, or stepping outside the Muslim scholarly tradition. The video's extension is the speaker's own added interpretation, not present in the (weak) text itself.

maudu.excerpt: Seek knowledge even if it were in China.
maudu.gradingNote: Classical commentators who discussed this saying at all (e.g. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, al-Munawi in Fayd al-Qadir) historically read 'China' as rhetorical hyperbole for how far a hadith-collector should travel to verify chains of transmission within the broader Muslim scholarly world of the era — not as an instruction to source religious knowledge from non-Muslims, which China at that time was not understood to offer. This undercuts the specific 'even amongst the non-Muslims' extension made in the video.

maudu.narrator: Verdict on the Anas ibn Malik narration
maudu.gradingNote: Since the foundational wording itself is judged fabricated, any interpretive extension built on top of it — including the claim that it sanctions seeking knowledge from non-Muslims — inherits that same weak evidentiary foundation rather than standing on independent textual support.
